newsitem.title: USA: Unocal found liable for selenium discharge.
newsitem.headline: Unocal found liable for selenium discharge.

text.p: A federal judge has ruled that Unocal Corp is liable under state and federal law for discharging excess selenium from a northern California oil refinery, court documents showed Thursday.

As a result of the ruling, Unocal could potentially be ordered to pay federal penalties of up to $50 million and tens of millions of dollars more in state penalties, according to Linda Dardarian, an attorney for environmental groups that sued Unocal over the discharges.
A spokesman for Unocal said the company was reviewing the ruling and had no comment.

U.S. District Judge Thelton Henderson, in a ruling issued Wednesday, granted the environmental groups' motion for summary judgment on the issue of Unocal's liability for alleged violations of the federal Clean Water Act and California Unfair Practices Act.

The environmental groups maintain that Unocal's Rodeo oil refinery in northern California discharges more selenium into San Pablo Bay than allowed by Unocal's National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permit. San Pablo Bay flows into San Francisco Bay.
Unocal recently sold the refinery to Tosco Corp.

Dardarian said the environmental groups' next step would be to submit evidence to Henderson on the penalty they believed he should assess against Unocal "and the amount of profit that Unocal wrongfully gained by violating the permit."
She said the groups would also seek an injunction requiring the refinery to "stop violating its permit and bring the discharges of selenium within the permitted levels."

Dardarian said the permit allowed Unocal to discharge 0.85 pounds per day of selenium into the bay but the refinery had been discharging about 5 pounds of selenium a day since the permit limit went into effect in December 1993.
Selenium, a byproduct of oil refining, is toxic in high concentrations.

In 1993, Unocal reached an agreement with the Regional Water Quality Control Board, which enforces federal water standards in the area, to postpone the deadline for the stricter selenium limits until 1998.
Unocal unsuccessfully tried to have the environmentalists' suit thrown out, saying that the agreement with the water board prevented lawsuits by private citizens.

If Henderson set penalties at trial, federal penalties would go to the U.S. Treasury, Dardarian said. But if the parties settled the suit, the environmental groups could choose cleanup projects that the money would be spent on, she said.
